speaker: Jim Keller
title: Jim Keller: Moore's Law, Microprocessors, and First Principles (#70)
question: In semiconductor manufacturing, why do domain experts repeatedly predict the imminent death of Moore's Law even as chip scaling keeps continuing?
guest: People think Moore's Law is one thing—transistors get smaller. But actually under the sheets there are literally thousands of innovations, and almost all of those innovations have their own diminishing return curves. If you graph it, it looks like a cascade of diminishing return curves, and the result is an exponential curve, at least it has been. We keep inventing new things, so if you're an expert in one of the things on a diminishing return curve and you can see its plateau, you will probably tell people, "Well, this is done." Meanwhile, some other pile of people are doing something different, so that's just normal. Then there's the observation of how small a switching device can be. A modern transistor is something like a thousand by a thousand by a thousand atoms, and you get quantum effects down around two to ten atoms. So you can imagine a transistor as small as ten by ten by ten, which is a million times smaller—and quantum computational people are working away at how to use quantum effects.

points.core: Moore's Law is powered by thousands of separate underlying technology innovations.
points.note: Accept: recognizing that Moore's Law is not a single scaling lever (just 2D shrinking) but a stack of many distinct lithography, materials, device, and process innovations. Do not credit: vague statements about human ingenuity.

points.core: Overlapping diminishing-return curves combine to produce an overall exponential scaling trend.
points.note: Accept: a cascade or sequence of individual S-curves / diminishing-return curves stacking together to sustain long-term exponential improvement. Do not credit: merely defining exponential growth.

points.core: Specialists mistake their own sub-technology's plateau for an industry-wide physical wall.
points.note: Accept: domain experts watching their specific technique (e.g. a lithography or transistor geometry) hit diminishing returns and extrapolating that the entire law is over while other groups introduce new curves. Do not credit: claiming experts are simply pessimistic or wrong without explaining the local-curve blind spot.

points.core: Modern transistors remain orders of magnitude larger than the atomic quantum-limit floor.
points.note: Accept: noting that current transistors still span millions or billions of atoms while quantum tunneling limits hit at a few atoms (~2–10 atoms per side), leaving substantial physical headroom. Do not credit: claiming quantum computing will replace classical silicon CMOS.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Experts keep predicting the end because each one sees, correctly, that the technique currently driving scaling is about to hit a physical or economic wall. What they cannot see is the next workaround, which usually comes from outside their specialty.

The history bears this out. Optical lithography was supposed to fail near one micron, yet immersion, multiple patterning and then EUV extended it. Gate oxide leakage was solved by high-k metal gates, and short-channel effects by FinFETs and now gate-all-around transistors. Each forecast was an accurate extrapolation of a single approach, not of the industry's ingenuity.

There is also a self-fulfilling element. Moore's Law is an economic coordination target, not a law of nature, so warnings of its demise mobilize enormous R&D spending and roadmaps aimed precisely at averting it.

Finally, the goalposts move. Classic Dennard scaling did end around 2005, cost per transistor has stopped falling as quickly, and node names like "3 nm" no longer describe physical dimensions. Progress now comes from new materials, 3D stacking and advanced packaging, so pessimists and optimists are both partly right, depending on which definition they use.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Domain experts repeatedly predict the end of Moore’s Law because each manufacturing paradigm genuinely hits hard physical and economic walls before its successor is proven viable, and because "Moore’s Law" itself keeps getting redefined. Looking a decade ahead, engineers confront real bottlenecks—such as optical diffraction limits, quantum tunneling, heat dissipation, and soaring fab costs—with no guaranteed commercial fix in sight. Paradoxically, sounding the alarm acts as a catalyst, mobilizing billions in R&D across the industry to invent discontinuous breakthroughs like high-k metal gates, FinFETs, extreme ultraviolet lithography, gate-all-around nanosheets, and 3D packaging. Meanwhile, skeptics and optimists often define scaling differently. Strict two-dimensional feature shrinking, Dennard power scaling, and falling cost per transistor have already stalled or ended, making many past warnings technically accurate. Yet chipmakers continue delivering effective density and performance gains through vertical stacking, chiplets, and design-technology co-optimization—repeatedly moving the goalposts of what counts as keeping Moore’s Law alive.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Experts keep predicting the end because they correctly see that the current way of scaling is running out. They're wrong about the end because the industry keeps switching to new ways.

Each era runs into real physical limits that are visible years ahead: optical lithography reaching its wavelength limit, gate oxides only a few atoms thick, leakage current, heat density, and quantum tunneling. Extrapolating from known techniques, the wall looks close, and for that specific technique it usually is. Engineers then get around it with something new: immersion lithography, multipatterning, EUV, high-k metal gates, strained silicon, FinFETs, gate-all-around transistors, backside power, 3D stacking and chiplets. Hard-to-predict innovation keeps beating straight-line pessimism.

Moore's Law is also partly self-fulfilling. It's an economic roadmap the whole industry coordinates around and puts hundreds of billions of dollars toward, not a law of nature.

The pessimists have also been partly right. Dennard scaling, where shrinking transistors also cut power use, ended around 2005, which stalled clock speeds. Cost per transistor has largely stopped falling at leading nodes. Node names like "3nm" are now marketing labels rather than real dimensions. So "Moore's Law continues" often means transistor density keeps rising, but more slowly, at higher cost, and under looser definitions. Both sides can claim to be right.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Domain experts repeatedly predict the death of Moore's Law because they evaluate the hard physical limits of today's manufacturing paradigm, whereas the industry continually survives by changing the paradigm itself. At any given generation, engineers face genuinely insurmountable walls—whether optical diffraction limits, quantum tunneling through thin oxides, or runaway heat after Dennard scaling ended. Extrapolating existing techniques honestly shows that scaling must stop. Yet massive economic incentives consistently fund breakthroughs that bypass those barriers, from immersion and extreme ultraviolet lithography to high-k metal gates, FinFETs, gate-all-around nanosheets, and backside power delivery.

The debate also persists because Moore's Law is an economic observation about cost-effective transistor density, not a single physical mechanism. In the narrow sense of cheap, purely two-dimensional transistor shrinking, experts are often right that classical scaling has slowed or ended. However, the industry keeps effective scaling alive by shifting to three-dimensional stacking, chiplets, and advanced packaging. Each prediction accurately diagnoses the end of the current roadmap, while underestimating the industry's ability to invent a new one.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Experts can correctly see that a particular way of shrinking transistors is running out of room and still underestimate how long chip scaling can continue. As features shrink, problems such as leakage, heat, and lithography become harder to solve. The limits of today’s manufacturing process are easier to measure than the gains from a technology that hasn’t reached mass production. New transistor designs and fabrication techniques have repeatedly moved those limits.

“Moore’s Law” also gets used to mean several things that once improved together. Transistor counts can keep rising even as clock speeds level off, the cost per transistor falls more slowly, and new manufacturing nodes take longer to arrive. So some predictions of its death correctly identify the end of a specific benefit or the old doubling pace, even while manufacturers keep finding ways to fit more transistors on a chip.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Experts often see a real limit to the manufacturing method they know best. Looking a few chip generations ahead, they can explain precisely why a transistor design will leak too much current or why a lithography tool will struggle to print smaller features. It’s harder to predict when a replacement will become reliable and cheap enough for mass production. The forecasting error is treating the limit of today’s method as the limit of scaling itself.

Moore’s Law is an economic and engineering trend, and the industry also uses it as a target. The prospect of hitting a wall focuses investment on ways around it. FinFETs, for example, gave manufacturers better control over current as transistors shrank. Some predictions have also proved right in a narrower sense: transistor counts have continued to rise even as clock speeds and cost per transistor have stopped improving at their old rates.
